results.claim: His published client sent our paired-write fixture over real HTTP and ten checks passed, five of them controls.
After a restarted sender resent the old record's exact bytes, the current value was still the new one.
The $id inside our schema_v0 named inspeximus/schema_v0.json while the file is at research/schema_v0.json, so it returned 404.
Our effective_value is value times 0.5 to the power of age over half_life with the clock reset on access, so it is time dependent and a re-emit changes the bytes under one source id.
His fixtures omit effective_value and our schema marks it optional, so omitting it on the wire is conformant.
His client raises SourceConflict before any network call when the same source id is enqueued with different content.
His receiver answers 409 for changed content under an existing id when the sender has no local record of that id.
A bitemporal ledger keeps the earlier record in history, and an erasure request requires that record not to remain.
Our draft carries three operations where schema_v0 has one: superseded, retracted and erased.
The erasure extension is two endpoints, POST /mnemo/v0/erase and POST /mnemo/v0/still_recoverable, matching the ErasureTarget protocol inspeximus already implements.
Two partner fixtures answered identical erase requests and both reported an erased count of 2.
The honest partner produced a complete deletion manifest and the lying partner produced an incomplete manifest naming the leaking store.
The erased count did not separate the two partners; only the post-erasure recheck did.
schema_v0 carries sources as channel and principal, and inspeximus refuses a source without a doc key because doc is what erasure resolves on.
Adding doc alongside channel and principal is the only schema_v1 change this proposal requires.
